paragraphs: SWAG addresses how a neural network can represent uncertainty about its predictions. It builds on Stochastic Weight Averaging, which averages the weights visited during training with a modified learning-rate schedule. Instead of using that average as a single final model, SWAG makes it the center of a probability distribution over possible network weights.

The method fits a Gaussian distribution whose covariance also comes from the training trajectory. Its low-rank component represents coordinated variation among weights, while its diagonal component provides additional per-weight variation. Sampling weights from this distribution and combining their predictions implements an approximate form of Bayesian model averaging. The construction therefore extracts uncertainty information from the same sequence of weights used to form the average.

The authors empirically find that this Gaussian approximates the shape of the true posterior. They also report good performance across calibration, out-of-sample detection, and transfer learning compared with several popular alternatives. These findings support SWAG as a simple, scalable uncertainty method, while retaining its status as a posterior approximation.
neurips-2019-a-simple-baseline-for-bayes.tldr: SWAG estimates uncertainty by fitting a Gaussian to training-time network weights and averaging predictions from sampled models.

paragraphs: Empowerment motivates an agent to reach situations where it has many possible ways to influence what happens next. This paper studies how that intrinsic motivation can work alongside an externally supplied reward. The authors hypothesize that seeking empowered states can help an agent discover useful behavior early in learning, while it is still learning how to obtain task rewards.

They formulate a unified Bellman optimality principle that combines empowerment with reward maximization. The principle generalizes both the conventional reward-based formulation and recent information-theoretic extensions. For this formulation, the authors prove that the empowered values are unique and establish convergence to the optimal solution. This gives the combined objective a mathematical foundation beyond simply adding an informal exploration preference.

The authors then develop off-policy actor-critic algorithms and evaluate them in high-dimensional continuous robotics tasks in MuJoCo. The methods show better initial performance and competitive final performance against model-free state-of-the-art techniques. The empirical result supports the proposed early-learning benefit without claiming uniformly superior final performance.
neurips-2019-a-unified-bellman-optimalit.tldr: A unified reinforcement-learning objective combines reward with empowerment and yields improved early performance in continuous robotics experiments.

paragraphs: Multi-view learning combines different descriptions of the same samples, but those descriptions can have complicated relationships and some may be missing. CPM-Nets addresses how to learn a useful shared representation under these conditions. Its aim is to capture both information that views share and information that individual views contribute.

The authors formally define completeness and versatility for multi-view representations, then prove versatility for the representation learned by their algorithm. To pursue completeness, they recast representation learning as a degradation process that mimics data transmission. This formulation is designed to balance agreement between views with their complementary information, rather than treating agreement alone as the goal.

The framework uses all samples and all available views, instead of organizing learning around completed missing views or separate missingness groups. It also produces a structured representation intended to support interpretability. Extensive experiments report effectiveness relative to existing state-of-the-art methods. Together, the theoretical and empirical contributions address different aspects of the proposal: a formal property of the representation and its usefulness in evaluated tasks.
neurips-2019-cpm-nets-cross-partial-mult.tldr: CPM-Nets learns structured representations from incomplete multi-view data by balancing shared and complementary information across views.

paragraphs: The lottery ticket result showed that pruning a network by retaining large weights can uncover sparse networks that train successfully from their original initialization. Those sparse networks can even outperform the full network. This paper investigates which parts of that procedure account for its success, rather than treating pruning and initialization as an indivisible recipe.

The authors vary three critical components of the lottery ticket algorithm and find considerable flexibility without losing its overall results. Their analysis explains the importance of setting weights to zero and shows that preserving weight signs can be sufficient to make a reinitialized network train. It also examines how choosing a mask can itself behave like training, because the choice determines which connections participate.

The strongest illustration is the discovery of Supermasks: masks that give an untrained, randomly initialized network performance well above chance. The reported results are 86% on MNIST and 41% on CIFAR-10. These findings show that selecting connections can encode substantial predictive structure even when the underlying random weights remain untrained.
neurips-2019-deconstructing-lottery-tick.tldr: Experiments unpack why lottery ticket pruning works and reveal masks that make randomly initialized networks perform well above chance.

paragraphs: An agent can learn more than the answer to its main task: additional prediction problems can help it develop useful internal representations. This paper asks whether the agent can discover those auxiliary questions itself. It expresses questions as general value functions, a flexible form of knowledge representation within reinforcement learning.

The method learns which questions to ask using non-myopic meta-gradients. The guiding criterion is whether learning their answers produces representations that help the main task. This connects the design of an auxiliary task to its downstream learning consequences, rather than selecting it solely because it appears sensible to a human designer.

The authors demonstrate that the discovered auxiliary tasks can, on their own, build representations sufficient for main-task learning. In their evaluations, these representations work better than those produced by popular hand-designed auxiliary tasks. They also show that learning such tasks alongside the main objective can improve an actor-critic agent's data efficiency on Atari2600 games. The findings support discovering useful learning objectives as part of the agent's own training process.
neurips-2019-discovery-of-useful-questio.tldr: An agent learns its own auxiliary prediction questions by optimizing how much their answers help it learn the main task.

paragraphs: This paper studies non-convex optimization when an algorithm can evaluate an objective but cannot directly obtain its gradients. Such derivative-free methods can estimate gradients from finite differences. The central question is whether these estimates allow algorithms to avoid saddle points efficiently, rather than merely reach places where first-order changes are small.

For a broad range of finite-difference gradient approximators, the authors establish asymptotic convergence to second-order stationary points. Their argument uses a tailored application of the Stable Manifold Theorem. They also introduce a noisy zero-order algorithm with a convergence-rate guarantee, extending the contribution from eventual behavior to the amount of optimization work required.

The noisy method requires approximately an inverse-square number of approximate gradient calculations in the target accuracy, with logarithmic factors suppressed. Its guarantee matches the corresponding exact-gradient rate up to constants as stated in the abstract. The analysis avoids additional dimension-dependent penalties in iteration count. This distinction concerns iterations and approximate gradient calculations; it does not claim that every gradient approximation has dimension-independent evaluation cost.
neurips-2019-efficiently-avoiding-saddle.tldr: The paper proves saddle-avoidance guarantees for finite-difference methods and introduces a noisy algorithm with efficient iteration bounds.

paragraphs: CNAPs tackles image classification when a system must adapt to new tasks after an initial period of training across multiple tasks. The challenge is to transfer what it has learned while accommodating the particular examples available for the current task. Those examples may be scarce or comparatively plentiful.

The system pairs a classifier with an adaptation network. Given the current task's dataset, the adaptation network modulates the classifier's parameters. This conditional neural process approach connects task adaptation with meta-learning and few-shot learning. Because adaptation does not require gradient-based updates at test time, the model can produce a task-specific classifier without an additional gradient optimization procedure.

The authors report state-of-the-art results on Meta-Dataset and robustness across both low-shot and high-shot settings, avoiding the respective problems of overfitting and underfitting in their evaluations. Timing experiments support test-time efficiency. They also demonstrate that trained models can be used directly for continual and active learning, where they can outperform approaches that do not use transfer learning. These findings connect adaptable representations with practical deployment across several learning settings.
neurips-2019-fast-and-flexible-multi-tas.tldr: CNAPs adapts image classifiers to new tasks through a dataset-conditioned network, avoiding gradient-based adaptation at test time.

paragraphs: Convolutional networks build assumptions about spatial structure into their architecture. This paper investigates how those assumptions influence training by mapping a convolutional network into an equivalent fully connected network. The mapping lets the authors compare both forms of training within the same fully connected parameter space.

Their protocol first trains a convolutional network, converts it at a chosen relaxation time, and then continues training as a fully connected network. Across the relaxation times studied, the converted network remains close to the convolutional subspace and finishes with better performance than a conventionally trained fully connected network of the same architecture. At some intermediate relaxation times, it also outperforms the originating convolutional network.

These observations suggest that early convolutional structure can guide optimization toward regions with strong generalization, while later flexibility can provide additional benefit. The authors interpret the results as evidence that architectural bias persists under stochastic gradient training. They also identify a practical constraint: the equivalent fully connected network is very large and highly sparse, limiting the protocol's usefulness as a routine training method.
neurips-2019-finding-the-needle-in-the-h.tldr: Convolutional training can guide an equivalent fully connected network toward better solutions, with benefits persisting after architectural constraints are relaxed.

paragraphs: Memory faults can threaten the reliability of convolutional-network inference, an important concern for applications such as autonomous vehicles and aerospace. Conventional protection methods include error-correcting codes and triple modular redundancy. The paper identifies their substantial memory overhead and energy cost as a motivation for protection designed specifically around convolutional networks.

The proposed method combines in-place error correction with a new training scheme called weight distribution-oriented training. Training is therefore part of the protection strategy, rather than leaving memory reliability entirely to a separate mechanism that ignores the network. The two components are presented together as a way to provide error correction without allocating additional space for protection.

The authors claim the first known CNN memory-protection method with zero space cost that preserves the reliability offered by traditional error-correcting codes. The significance is the combination of those two properties: eliminating extra protection storage while retaining the stated reliability level. The zero-cost claim is specifically about space, so it should be understood as a memory result rather than a claim that every computational or energy cost disappears.
neurips-2019-in-place-zero-space-memory-.tldr: The paper combines in-place error correction with weight distribution-oriented training to protect CNN memory without additional space cost.

paragraphs: Following visual content through a video requires both a broad understanding of where an object or region moves and precise matches between individual pixels. This paper learns these two kinds of correspondence together through self-supervision. Its goal is reliable dense matching between consecutive frames without relying on supervised correspondence training.

The method links region tracking and pixel matching through a shared inter-frame affinity matrix, which represents associations across frames at both scales. Region-level localization narrows the area where a pixel match should be sought, reducing ambiguity. In the other direction, fine-grained matches provide features that help locate larger regions. Each task therefore supplies information that supports the other.

The authors report improvements over state-of-the-art self-supervised methods on segmentation propagation, keypoint tracking, and object tracking. They also report surpassing the supervised affinity representation from an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-18. That comparison concerns the stated representation and evaluated correspondence tasks. The broader contribution is evidence that coordinating coarse and fine temporal matching can produce strong correspondence features from self-supervised learning.
neurips-2019-joint-task-self-supervised-.tldr: Jointly learning region tracking and pixel matching improves self-supervised video correspondence through a shared cross-frame affinity representation.

paragraphs: Proving polynomial inequalities automatically requires finding useful sequences of mathematical deductions. The paper works within semi-algebraic proof systems, where elementary inference rules derive new polynomial inequalities from existing premises. These systems are powerful, but deciding which deductions to pursue creates a difficult search problem.

The authors introduce a deep reinforcement-learning method that guides this search toward dynamic proofs. It learns representations of polynomials and uses them to select inference rules. The model also incorporates inherent problem symmetries as an inductive bias, allowing the structure of the mathematical task to influence how proof-search decisions are learned.

The approach is compared with established linear-programming hierarchies based on static proof systems. In the reported comparisons, it reduces the size of the linear program by several orders of magnitude while improving performance. The result suggests that learned guidance can make powerful proof machinery more effective by directing which deductions are constructed. The contribution concerns learning how to search within these systems, with the inference rules still defining the mathematical steps available.
neurips-2019-learning-dynamic-polynomial.tldr: A reinforcement-learning system guides polynomial proof search, reducing linear-program size by orders of magnitude in reported comparisons.

paragraphs: Learning fair behavior in a multi-agent system is difficult because agents must balance fairness with efficiency while their policies interact. FEN addresses this as a joint learning problem. The method first decomposes fairness at the level of individual agents and gives each agent a reward that combines fairness and efficiency.

Each agent uses a hierarchical policy rather than a single undifferentiated behavior. A controller chooses among several sub-policies, which provide different ways to interact with the environment. The controller learns to maximize the combined fair-efficient reward by switching between these behaviors. This division is designed to reduce conflict between the objectives while preserving behavioral variety.

FEN can be trained in a fully decentralized manner, which the authors identify as helpful for real-world deployment. Their experiments report that it learns both fairness and efficiency and significantly outperforms the evaluated baselines across varied multi-agent scenarios. The findings support hierarchical control as a practical way to coordinate competing learning objectives in those settings, rather than establishing a universal guarantee of fair outcomes.
neurips-2019-learning-fairness-in-multi-.tldr: FEN uses decentralized hierarchical reinforcement learning to balance fairness and efficiency by switching among diverse agent behaviors.

paragraphs: Boolean satisfiability asks whether truth values can be assigned to variables so that a collection of logical requirements is satisfied. Local search approaches this by repeatedly changing a candidate assignment. A central choice is which variable to change next, and this paper investigates learning that choice instead of relying on a generic handcrafted heuristic.

The authors place a graph neural network inside a stochastic local-search algorithm to serve as its variable-selection heuristic. They train it from scratch with deep reinforcement learning and a curriculum. They consider several classes of satisfiability problems and learn a specialized heuristic for each class, making the target the structure of a problem family rather than a single universal selection rule.

Experiments show that the learned heuristics find satisfying assignments in fewer search steps than a generic heuristic. The authors explicitly do not aim to compete with state-of-the-art solvers on runtime. The supported result is therefore improved search-step efficiency in the studied settings, demonstrating that learned choices can guide local search more effectively without establishing faster overall solving.
neurips-2019-learning-local-search-heuri.tldr: Graph neural networks learn problem-class-specific SAT search heuristics that find satisfying assignments in fewer steps than a generic heuristic.

paragraphs: Persistent homology produces summaries of data's topological structure, commonly represented as persistence diagrams. To use these summaries in machine learning, methods often convert them into vectors and assign different importance to different persistence features. This paper questions the use of fixed importance weights when the useful features may depend on the particular labeled dataset.

The authors introduce a weighted kernel called WKPI and an optimization framework for learning its weights. A kernel determines how summaries are compared, so learning these weights also learns a task-informed notion of similarity. This allows labels to influence which aspects of the topological representation matter most for the prediction problem.

They apply the learned kernel to graph classification and evaluate it on a collection of benchmark datasets. The resulting framework matches or improves on the best results from a range of earlier graph-classification approaches, with improvements sometimes significant. The findings support adapting persistence-feature weights to the data, while preserving the qualified result that performance is comparable in some cases and better in others.
neurips-2019-learning-metrics-for-persis.tldr: WKPI learns how to weight topological features from labeled data, producing competitive and sometimes significantly better graph classification results.

paragraphs: Clustering time series requires representations that preserve temporal patterns while making similar sequences easy to group. Handcrafted features can help, but they depend on domain knowledge. This paper proposes Deep Temporal Clustering Representation, or DTCR, to learn cluster-oriented features without category labels.

DTCR combines a sequence-to-sequence model's temporal reconstruction objective with a K-means objective. Reconstruction encourages the representation to retain information about the sequence, while the clustering objective encourages a structure suited to grouping sequences. The authors also introduce generated fake samples and an auxiliary classification task to strengthen the encoder. These additions provide another learning signal within the unsupervised representation-learning framework.

Across extensive time-series experiments, the authors report state-of-the-art performance relative to existing methods. Their visualizations support the usefulness of the cluster-specific representations and show a robust learning process even when K-means makes mistakes. The result suggests that jointly shaping representations and clusters can be effective, instead of assuming a representation learned for reconstruction alone will automatically have the desired clustering structure.
neurips-2019-learning-representations-fo.tldr: DTCR jointly learns temporal reconstruction and clustering objectives to produce time-series representations suited to unsupervised grouping.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to learn discrete probability distributions with sparse structure using iterative hard thresholding. IHT alternates a gradient-based update with a projection that enforces the desired structure. Although it is successful in several structured estimation problems, applying it to distributions introduces constraints beyond selecting a sparse collection of ordinary parameters.

A probability distribution must satisfy the simplex constraint: its probabilities are nonnegative and sum to one. The authors study the difficulty of using IHT in the space of measures and propose a greedy approximate projection as a practical alternative. This projection is designed to respect both the relevant notion of distributional sparsity and the requirements for valid probabilities.

The authors investigate convergence of the resulting procedure in several settings and report theoretical and practical results showing that IHT can achieve state-of-the-art performance for sparse distribution learning. The contribution is therefore both algorithmic and analytical: a workable projection procedure and an examination of its behavior. The stated success is a possibility supported by their results, rather than a claim that the approximation always yields the best distribution.
neurips-2019-learning-sparse-distributio.tldr: A greedy approximate projection adapts iterative hard thresholding to sparse probability distributions while maintaining valid probability constraints.

paragraphs: Many combinatorial optimization methods improve a current solution through a sequence of local changes. Their effectiveness depends on heuristics that can be time-consuming to tune across situations. NeuRewriter learns how to choose those changes, repeatedly rewriting parts of a solution to improve it until convergence.

The policy separates each decision into two parts: selecting a region of the current solution and selecting a rewriting rule for that region. Each component is represented by a neural network trained with actor-critic reinforcement learning. This decomposition matches the structure of local improvement: deciding where to act and then deciding what action to take.

The authors evaluate the approach on expression simplification, online job scheduling, and vehicle routing. They report outperforming Z3's expression simplification component; DeepRM and Google OR-tools for scheduling; and recent neural baselines and Google OR-tools for routing. These task-specific findings support the usefulness of a shared local-rewriting framework across different problems. They do not equate convergence of iterative improvement with a guarantee of finding the globally optimal solution.
neurips-2019-learning-to-perform-local-r.tldr: NeuRewriter learns where and how to make local changes, improving solutions across expression simplification, scheduling, and vehicle routing.

paragraphs: The paper proposes an online predictor for discrete labels given several continuous features. Its goal is to learn a flexible relationship between features and labels while keeping the work required for each new observation small. The predictor does not rely on a fixed parametric form for that relationship.

It partitions feature space with a k-d tree using randomly selected directions and combines this partition with a recursive Bayesian distribution. The construction automatically learns which feature scales are relevant to the conditional label distribution. This makes the choice of resolution part of learning, rather than requiring a single predetermined discretization.

The authors prove pointwise universality: asymptotically, normalized log loss becomes as good as the true conditional entropy of labels given features. They also show that processing the nth observation takes logarithmic time in probability under the data-generating distribution. This is a probabilistic complexity statement, not a worst-case bound for every observation. Experiments on challenging datasets support both computational and statistical efficiency relative to standard and state-of-the-art alternatives.
neurips-2019-low-complexity-nonparametri.tldr: A tree-based Bayesian online predictor combines asymptotically optimal normalized log loss with logarithmic per-sample processing time in probability.

paragraphs: Regret measures the accumulated cost of learning instead of already following an optimal policy. This paper analyzes that cost for optimistic algorithms in episodic tabular Markov decision processes. Its main result gives logarithmic regret bounds that depend on the gaps separating optimal and inferior decisions, and that apply at finite learning horizons.

The bounds smoothly connect this gap-dependent behavior with a minimax rate proportional to the square root of HSAT, up to logarithmic factors. This connects a more problem-sensitive guarantee with the broader worst-case rate. Unlike earlier work described in the abstract, the analysis does not introduce dependence on diameter-like quantities or require ergodicity.

The key technical contribution is a clipped regret decomposition, a new way to break down the accumulated learning cost. It applies to a broad family of recent optimistic episodic algorithms, rather than only one specially constructed method. The significance is an improved explanation of when these algorithms can learn with logarithmically growing regret while retaining a connection to their worst-case guarantees.
neurips-2019-non-asymptotic-gap-dependen.tldr: A clipped regret analysis gives optimistic episodic reinforcement-learning algorithms finite-time, gap-dependent logarithmic guarantees that connect smoothly to minimax rates.

paragraphs: Stochastic k-PCA seeks the leading eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a moment matrix from independent, identically distributed vector samples. In the distributed setting studied here, multiple machines each receive a local dataset and send a small summary to a central server. The aim is to recover what could be learned by processing all samples centrally.

The paper examines a slight modification of distributed averaging. The important design choices are what each machine summarizes and how the server combines those summaries. The authors prove improved bounds on the relationship between the number of samples per machine and the eigenvalue gaps. These gaps distinguish the leading directions the procedure is trying to recover.

The method also applies when the appropriate value of k is not known exactly, meaning the user does not already know where a nontrivial eigenvalue gap occurs. The authors identify this as a common practical issue not addressed by prior methods. Together, the results strengthen the theoretical sample requirements and extend applicability when the desired spectral cutoff is uncertain.
neurips-2019-on-distributed-averaging-fo.tldr: A modified distributed averaging method improves stochastic k-PCA bounds and accommodates uncertainty about the appropriate number of leading components.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to make learning algorithms provably robust to adversarial changes in their test-time inputs without making computation impractical. It asks both when efficient robust learning is possible and what price must be paid for that efficiency. Its main contribution is a connection between these questions and polynomial optimization.

Using that connection, the authors design computationally efficient robust algorithms with guarantees for linear classifiers and degree-two polynomial threshold functions. They also characterize the price of obtaining robustness efficiently for those hypothesis classes. The scope matters: these are guarantees for the specified model families, rather than a general solution for every deep network.

The same perspective yields efficient procedures for certifying robustness and constructing adversarial attacks on two-layer neural networks. Certification and attack generation address complementary questions: whether robustness can be established and how vulnerable inputs can be found. Experiments on real data demonstrate the effectiveness of the attacks. The paper thus combines theoretical learning guarantees with concrete methods for examining the robustness of another class of models.
neurips-2019-on-robustness-to-adversaria.tldr: Connecting adversarial robustness to polynomial optimization yields provable learning algorithms and principled certification and attack methods for specified model classes.

paragraphs: PasteGAN addresses image generation with control over both scene structure and individual object appearance. A scene graph specifies object arrangements and pairwise relationships, while supplied image crops determine how the objects should look. This gives the generator more detailed guidance than a description that only specifies the overall scene meaning.

A Crop Refining Network and an Object-Image Fuser combine objects and their relationships into a shared map. Multiple training losses encourage the generated image to respect the crops, follow the scene graph, and maintain visual quality. If crops are absent, a selector chooses compatible examples from an external object collection using information about the surrounding relationships in the graph.

On Visual Genome and COCO-Stuff, the authors report significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods in Inception Score, Diversity Score, and Fréchet Inception Distance. Further experiments demonstrate the ability to generate complex, varied images containing given objects. The contribution links explicit appearance choices with relational scene generation, supporting control over what objects look like as well as how they interact.
neurips-2019-pastegan-a-semi-parametric-.tldr: PasteGAN combines scene graphs with object image crops to generate images with controllable object appearances and relationships.

paragraphs: Knowledge graph reasoning predicts missing facts from observed relationships. Logic-based methods can express domain rules and uncertainty, but inference in Markov Logic Networks can be difficult. Embedding methods learn useful numerical representations of entities and relations, yet the approaches discussed in the abstract do not incorporate domain knowledge. pLogicNet combines these two forms of reasoning.

The model uses a Markov Logic Network with first-order rules to define a joint distribution over possible triplets. It optimizes the model through variational expectation-maximization. In the expectation step, a knowledge graph embedding model infers missing triplets. In the maximization step, the system updates rule weights using both observed triplets and predicted ones.

This alternating procedure lets embedding-based predictions contribute to learning how strongly logical rules should influence the model. It also places those predictions within a framework that explicitly represents rule-based knowledge and uncertainty. Experiments on multiple knowledge graphs demonstrate effectiveness against many competitive baselines. The contribution is a coordinated learning procedure that brings these complementary modeling capabilities into one system.
neurips-2019-probabilistic-logic-neural-.tldr: pLogicNet combines logical rules and knowledge graph embeddings through variational EM to infer missing facts and learn rule weights.

paragraphs: Neural Processes combine neural-network flexibility with ideas from Gaussian processes to model uncertain functions and predict quickly. This paper addresses situations where the underlying stochastic process itself changes over time. Ordinary Neural Processes do not explicitly represent the temporal dependencies across such a sequence of processes.

Sequential Neural Processes add a temporal state-transition model. This extends the modeling framework so that changes in the underlying process can be represented as part of a temporal sequence. The distinction matters for dynamic settings: the model must account for how the process evolves, in addition to predicting observations associated with it.

For dynamic three-dimensional scenes, the authors introduce Temporal Generative Query Networks as an application of this idea. They describe it, to their knowledge, as the first four-dimensional model capable of handling temporal dynamics of 3D scenes. Evaluations cover non-stationary regression and scene inference and rendering over time. The stated contribution is the extension to dynamic stochastic processes and its evaluation in these settings, rather than a reported numerical performance advantage.
neurips-2019-sequential-neural-processes.tldr: Sequential Neural Processes add temporal transitions to Neural Processes, enabling models of changing functions and dynamic 3D scenes.

paragraphs: A single-index model generates an outcome by applying an unknown function to one weighted combination of input features, then adding noise. This paper considers Gaussian inputs and a sparse, unit-length vector of weights. The statistical goal concerns recovering that hidden direction and identifying which coordinates contribute to it.

Prior work can use a generalized Lasso when the outcome has nonzero covariance with the hidden linear combination. The authors investigate the harder case where that covariance vanishes. They focus on a specific remaining signal: the outcome has positive covariance with the square of the hidden combination, even though its direct linear covariance is zero.

Within the statistical query model of computation, the authors show that computationally tractable algorithms cannot attain the information-theoretic minimax risk under these conditions. This separates what the available information permits from what efficient algorithms in that model can achieve. The result identifies a computational price associated with the specified nonlinearity, with its force tied to the Gaussian, sparsity, covariance, and computational-model assumptions.
neurips-2019-statistical-computational-t.tldr: Under specified covariance conditions, sparse single-index models exhibit a gap between statistically possible accuracy and efficient statistical-query computation.
